items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A device that produces a beam of electrons by thermionic emission from a hot cathode and accelerates them through a potential difference"?
options: magnetic force on a moving charge
items.answer: electron gun
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of electron gun.

items.stem: "An electron moves in the direction of the electric field lines." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The force on an electron is opposite to the field direction.
items.markingKey: The force on an electron is opposite to the field direction. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Elena is revising motion of charged particles in uniform electric fields. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A constant force perpendicular to the plates gives a parabolic path; circular paths occur in magnetic fields.
Doubling the speed of a proton in a magnetic field doubles its period.
A magnetic field can be used to speed up an electron beam.
An electron moves in the direction of the electric field lines.
items.answer: A constant force perpendicular to the plates gives a parabolic path; circular paths occur in magnetic fields.
items.markingKey: A. The other options are common misconceptions. A constant force perpendicular to the plates gives a parabolic path; circular paths occur in magnetic fields.

items.stem: An electron is accelerated from rest through 100 V. What is its final speed?
Plates 2.0 cm apart have 600 V across them. What is the acceleration of an electron between the plates?
items.markingKey: D. a = eV/(mₑd) = 5.27 × 10¹⁵ m s⁻².

items.stem: In Millikan’s oil-drop experiment, a drop is first held stationary between plates 8.0 mm apart by a p.d. of 2400 V. When the field is switched off it falls at a constant (terminal) speed, from which its mass is found to be 4.9 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg. (a) Determine the charge on the drop. (b) Deduce how many electronic charges it carries. (c) Explain why Millikan’s results supported the idea that charge is quantised, and comment on the controversy over his data selection.
items.answer: (a) q = mgd/V = 4.9 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 9.81 × 8.0 × 10⁻³/2400 = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; (b) 1 electronic charge; (c) all measured charges were integer multiples of 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; historians found that he excluded some drops from publication, raising questions about selective reporting (NOS: ethics of data).
items.markingKey: qV/d = mg (M1); q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (A1); n = q/e = 1 (A1); multiples of e (R1); data-selection issue discussed (R1).

items.stem: A proton and an electron enter the same uniform electric field. Which is correct?
options: they experience equal and opposite forces, but the electron accelerates much more
items.answer: they experience equal and opposite forces, but the electron accelerates much more
items.markingKey: B. F = eE for both; a = F/m.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "electron gun".
items.answer: A device that produces a beam of electrons by thermionic emission from a hot cathode and accelerates them through a potential difference
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a device that produces a beam of electrons by thermionic emission from a hot cathode and accelerates them through a potential difference. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between motion in a uniform gravitational field and motion in a uniform electric field.
items.answer: Both give constant acceleration and parabolic paths for perpendicular entry; in an electric field a = qE/m depends on the charge-to-mass ratio and may be in either direction, whereas in a gravitational field a = g for all masses.
items.markingKey: Both give constant acceleration and parabolic paths for perpendicular entry; in an electric field a = qE/m depends on the charge-to-mass ratio and may be in either direction, whereas in a gravitational field a = g for all masses. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why the speed gained by a charged particle accelerated from rest depends only on the p.d. and not on the plate separation.
items.answer: The work done by the field is qV regardless of the distance; a larger separation gives a smaller field but over a longer distance, so qEd = qV is unchanged.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The work done by the field is qV regardless of the distance; a larger separation gives a smaller field but over a longer distance, so qEd = qV is unchanged. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: An electron beam is deflected by a uniform electric field between parallel plates. Predict and explain how the deflection at the exit of the plates changes if the plate separation is doubled at the same voltage.
items.answer: The deflection halves, because E = V/d halves, so the acceleration halves.
items.markingKey: the deflection halves (A1); E = V/d halves, so the acceleration halves (R1).

items.stem: A proton and an α particle are accelerated from rest through the same p.d. The ratio of their kinetic energies Eₚ/E_α is
items.markingKey: C. Eₖ = qV and q_α = 2e.

items.stem: An α particle is accelerated from rest through a p.d. of 1000 V. Calculate its final speed.
items.markingKey: qV = ½mv² (M1); v = √(2qV/m) = 3.10 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem:
An electron beam of speed v passes between plates 4.0 cm long and 1.0 cm apart. The vertical deflection y at the exit is measured for different deflecting voltages V. Theory: y = eL²V/(2mₑdv²).

V / V | y / mm
20 | 0.46
40 | 0.90
60 | 1.37
80 | 1.76
100 | 2.22
120 | 2.71

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the speed v of the electrons. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±3 %. State the electron speed with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) y in m (y) against V (x); (b) gradient ≈ 2.23 × 10⁻⁵ m V⁻¹; (c) 2.51 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹; (d) 2.51 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ ± 8 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) y in m (y) against V (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 2.23 × 10⁻⁵ m V⁻¹ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) v = √(eL²/(2mₑd × gradient)) = 2.51 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 3 % of the value = 8 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: An α particle (charge +2e) is accelerated from rest through 200 V. What kinetic energy does it gain?
items.markingKey: B. Eₖ = qV = 2eV = 6.40 × 10⁻¹⁷ J.

items.stem: An electron is accelerated from rest through 500 V. What is its final speed?

In an oscilloscope tube, electrons are accelerated through 1000 V, then pass between deflecting plates 3.0 cm long and 1.0 cm apart with 60 V across them. The screen is 20 cm beyond the end of the plates. (a) Calculate the speed of the electrons entering the plates. (b) Calculate the deflection at the exit of the plates. (c) Determine the total deflection on the screen. (d) Explain why doubling the accelerating voltage halves the deflection.
items.markingKey: (a) v = √(2eV/m) = 1.87 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ (A1). (b) a = 1.05 × 10¹⁵ m s⁻², t = 1.60 × 10⁻⁹ s (M1), y = ½at² = 1.35 mm (A1). (c) straight line after plates: extra v_y·D/v (M1); total 19.4 mm (A1). (d) deflection ∝ 1/v² and v² ∝ V_a (R1).

items.stem: "Thomson’s cathode-ray experiments discovered the electron." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Thomson is credited because he interpreted measurements as evidence for a universal sub-atomic particle, but discovery built on earlier and later work.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: he measured e/m and showed it was the same for all cathode materials; his interpretation as a universal particle was new. Arguments against: many others (Crookes, Schuster, Kaufmann) worked on cathode rays; the charge was later measured by Millikan; discovery is a process involving a community (NOS). Supported judgement: Thomson is credited because he interpreted measurements as evidence for a universal sub-atomic particle, but discovery built on earlier and later work. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Why does the magnetic force do no work on a moving charge?
options: the charge is moving too fast
it is always perpendicular to the velocity
items.answer: it is always perpendicular to the velocity
items.markingKey: D. W = Fs cos 90° = 0, so speed is constant.

items.stem: Omar writes four statements while revising force on a moving charge and the circular motion of charges in magnetic fields. Which one is a misconception?
options: Doubling the speed of a proton in a magnetic field doubles its period.
The force is perpendicular to both the field and the current, as given by Fleming’s left-hand rule.
Both wires feel the same force μ₀I₁I₂L/(2πr), by Newton’s third law.
A stationary charge experiences no magnetic force (v = 0).
items.answer: Doubling the speed of a proton in a magnetic field doubles its period.
items.markingKey: A. This is incorrect: T = 2πm/(qB) is independent of speed; the radius doubles instead.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the force on a charge in a magnetic field and the force on a charge in an electric field.
items.answer: An electric force qE acts on any charge, moving or not, along the field, and can change speed; a magnetic force qvB sin θ acts only on moving charges, perpendicular to v and B, and changes only direction.
items.markingKey: An electric force qE acts on any charge, moving or not, along the field, and can change speed; a magnetic force qvB sin θ acts only on moving charges, perpendicular to v and B, and changes only direction. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Kenji writes: "A stationary electron in a magnetic field experiences a force along the field lines." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A stationary charge experiences no magnetic force (v = 0).
items.markingKey: A stationary charge experiences no magnetic force (v = 0). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A proton moves at 1.00 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a 0.2 T magnetic field. What is the radius of its path?

In a fine-beam tube, electrons accelerated through a p.d. V move in circles of radius r in a uniform magnetic field of 0.80 mT. Theory: r² = (2m/(eB²)) V.

V / V | r / cm
150 | 5.22
200 | 5.93
250 | 6.62
300 | 7.28
350 | 7.86
400 | 8.39

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the specific charge e/m of the electron. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±5 %. State e/m with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) r² in m² (y) against V (x); (b) gradient ≈ 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ m² V⁻¹; (c) 1.79 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹; (d) 1.79 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹ ± 9 × 10⁹ C kg⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) r² in m² (y) against V (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ m² V⁻¹ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) e/m = 2/(gradient × B²) = 1.79 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹ (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 5 % of the value = 9 × 10⁹ C kg⁻¹; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: An electron moving at 5.00 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ enters a uniform magnetic field of 0.00200 T with its velocity at 30° to the field lines. (a) Explain why its path is a helix. (b) Calculate the radius of the helix. (c) Calculate the distance it travels along the field in one revolution (the pitch).
items.markingKey: (a) component parallel to B (v cos θ) is unaffected; perpendicular component (v sin θ) gives circular motion (R1 R1). (b) r = mv sin θ/(eB) (M1) = 0.00712 m (A1). (c) T = 2πm/(eB) = 1.79 × 10⁻⁸ s; pitch = v cos θ × T (M1) = 0.0775 m (A1).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Mass spectrometry is the most reliable way to identify isotopes."
items.answer: Very powerful and widely used, but results need careful interpretation; overlaps mean it is best combined with other techniques.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: separates ions by m/q with high precision; needs only tiny samples. Arguments against: ions of the same m/q (e.g. different molecules) can overlap; requires ionisation and vacuum; nuclear methods give different information (e.g. decay). Supported judgement: Very powerful and widely used, but results need careful interpretation; overlaps mean it is best combined with other techniques. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "magnetic force on a moving charge"?
options: A pair of parallel plates with a p.d. between them that deflects a beam of charged particles passing between them
The force per unit length F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πr) between two long parallel wires; attractive for currents in the same direction
The force F = qvB sin θ on a charge q moving with velocity v at angle θ to a magnetic field B, perpendicular to both v and B
An instrument that separates ions by their mass-to-charge ratio using the radius of their circular paths in a magnetic field
items.answer: The force F = qvB sin θ on a charge q moving with velocity v at angle θ to a magnetic field B, perpendicular to both v and B
items.markingKey: C. "magnetic force on a moving charge" is the force F = qvB sin θ on a charge q moving with velocity v at angle θ to a magnetic field B, perpendicular to both v and B.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The force F = qvB sin θ on a charge q moving with velocity v at angle θ to a magnetic field B, perpendicular to both v and B"?
options: magnetic force on a moving charge
items.answer: magnetic force on a moving charge
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of magnetic force on a moving charge.

items.stem: A beam of positive ions passes undeflected through crossed E and B fields. Faster ions in the beam will be
options: deflected in the direction of the electric force
deflected in the direction of the magnetic force
items.answer: deflected in the direction of the magnetic force
items.markingKey: B. For v > E/B, qvB > qE.

items.stem: Explain why a charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field moves in a circle.
items.answer: The magnetic force qvB is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes the direction but not the speed; a force of constant magnitude always perpendicular to the velocity provides a centripetal force, giving uniform circular motion.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The magnetic force qvB is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes the direction but not the speed; a force of constant magnitude always perpendicular to the velocity provides a centripetal force, giving uniform circular motion. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "A magnetic field can be used to speed up an electron beam." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity and does no work, so it cannot change the speed; an electric field is needed.
items.markingKey: The magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity and does no work, so it cannot change the speed; an electric field is needed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student in Singapore is checking notes on force on a moving charge and the circular motion of charges in magnetic fields. Which statement is incorrect?
options: The force is perpendicular to both the field and the current, as given by Fleming’s left-hand rule.
A constant force perpendicular to the plates gives a parabolic path; circular paths occur in magnetic fields.
The force on an electron is opposite to the field direction.
A stationary electron in a magnetic field experiences a force along the field lines.
items.answer: A stationary electron in a magnetic field experiences a force along the field lines.
items.markingKey: D. This is incorrect: A stationary charge experiences no magnetic force (v = 0).

items.stem: Explain how crossed electric and magnetic fields select particles of one speed.
items.answer: The electric force qE and magnetic force qvB act in opposite directions; they balance only when v = E/B, so only particles of that speed pass undeflected; faster particles are deflected by the magnetic force, slower by the electric force.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The electric force qE and magnetic force qvB act in opposite directions; they balance only when v = E/B, so only particles of that speed pass undeflected; faster particles are deflected by the magnetic force, slower by the electric force. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Calculate the period and frequency of the circular motion of an electron in a uniform magnetic field of 0.0100 T.

In a velocity selector the magnetic flux density is 0.0200 T. Calculate the electric field strength needed for protons travelling at 1.50 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ to pass undeflected, and explain why the result does not depend on the charge.
items.markingKey: qE = qvB (M1); E = vB = 3.00 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹ (A1); q cancels, so selection depends only on speed (R1).

items.stem: A cyclotron accelerates protons between two D-shaped electrodes in a uniform magnetic field of 1.5 T; the D radius is 0.50 m. (a) Show that the frequency of the alternating voltage must be about 23 MHz. (b) Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the protons in MeV. (c) Explain why this design fails for electrons accelerated to similar energies.
items.answer: (a) f = qB/(2πm) = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1.5/(2π × 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷) = 2.3 × 10⁷ Hz; (b) v = qBR/m = 7.2 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹; Eₖ = ½mv² = 4.3 × 10⁻¹² J = 27 MeV; (c) electrons become relativistic at much lower energies, their mass effectively increases, so the frequency changes and they fall out of step.
items.markingKey: f = qB/2πm (M1) value (A1); v_max = qBR/m (M1); Eₖ ≈ 27 MeV (A1); relativistic argument (R1).

items.stem: In a Bainbridge mass spectrometer, singly charged ions first pass through a velocity selector with E = 6.00 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ and B = 0.20 T, then enter a region of uniform field 0.40 T where they travel in semicircles onto a detector. (a) Calculate the speed of the selected ions. (b) Calculate the radii of the paths of chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 ions. (c) Determine their separation on the detector. (d) Explain why the velocity selector is essential.
items.answer: (a) 3.00 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹; (b) 0.273 m and 0.288 m; (c) 31.1 mm; (d) r depends on v as well as m, so only with one speed is r ∝ m

items.stem: In a Bainbridge mass spectrometer, singly charged ions first pass through a velocity selector with E = 4.00 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ and B = 0.10 T, then enter a region of uniform field 0.25 T where they travel in semicircles onto a detector. (a) Calculate the speed of the selected ions. (b) Calculate the radii of the paths of magnesium-24 and magnesium-26 ions. (c) Determine their separation on the detector. (d) Explain why the velocity selector is essential.
items.answer: (a) 4.00 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹; (b) 0.399 m and 0.432 m; (c) 66.4 mm; (d) r depends on v as well as m, so only with one speed is r ∝ m

items.stem: An electron moving at 4.00 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ enters a uniform magnetic field of 0.00100 T with its velocity at 20° to the field lines. (a) Explain why its path is a helix. (b) Calculate the radius of the helix. (c) Calculate the distance it travels along the field in one revolution (the pitch).
items.markingKey: (a) component parallel to B (v cos θ) is unaffected; perpendicular component (v sin θ) gives circular motion (R1 R1). (b) r = mv sin θ/(eB) (M1) = 0.00779 m (A1). (c) T = 2πm/(eB) = 3.58 × 10⁻⁸ s; pitch = v cos θ × T (M1) = 0.134 m (A1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The force F = BIL sin θ on a length L of wire carrying current I at angle θ to a magnetic field B"?
items.answer: force on a current-carrying conductor
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of force on a current-carrying conductor.

items.stem: In an investigation the relationship F/L = μ₀I²/(2πr) for two parallel wires carrying the same current I is expected. Explain how a linear graph can be used to verify this relationship and to determine a value from the gradient.
items.answer: Plot F/L (y-axis) against I² (x-axis); gradient = μ₀/(2πr). A straight line through the origin confirms F ∝ I².
items.markingKey: Correct choice of axes: F/L against I² (M1); straight line expected (R1); gradient = μ₀/(2πr) (A1). A straight line through the origin confirms F ∝ I².

items.stem: A vertical wire carries current upwards in a horizontal magnetic field pointing north. The force on the wire is towards the
items.answer: west
items.markingKey: A. Fleming’s left-hand rule: field N, current up → force W.

items.stem: A wire 10 cm long carries 2 A at 30° to a 0.1 T field. What is the force on it?
items.markingKey: B. F = BIL sin θ = 0.0100 N.

items.stem: Omar writes: "If one wire carries twice the current of the other, it feels twice the force." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Both wires feel the same force μ₀I₁I₂L/(2πr), by Newton’s third law.
items.markingKey: Both wires feel the same force μ₀I₁I₂L/(2πr), by Newton’s third law. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A rectangular coil of 200 turns, with sides 5.0 cm (perpendicular to the field) and 3.0 cm, carries 1.0 A in a uniform field of 0.10 T. The plane of the coil is parallel to the field. (a) Calculate the force on each 5.0 cm side. (b) Calculate the maximum torque on the coil. (c) Explain why the torque falls to zero when the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field, and why a commutator is needed.
items.answer: (a) 1.00 N; (b) 0.0300 N m; (c) forces then act along the same line (no moment); the commutator reverses the current every half turn to keep rotation in one direction
items.markingKey: (a) F = NBIL (M1) = 1.00 N (A1). (b) torque = F × 3.0 cm = 0.0300 N m (M1 A1). (c) forces collinear/perpendicular distance zero (R1); current reversal maintains rotation (R1).

items.stem: Since 2019 the ampere is defined by
options: fixing the numerical value of the elementary charge e
the mass of the international prototype kilogram
items.answer: fixing the numerical value of the elementary charge e

items.stem: Briefly explain why two parallel wires carrying currents in opposite directions repel.
items.answer: Each wire is in the magnetic field of the other; using the right-hand grip rule for one wire and Fleming’s left-hand rule for the other shows the force on each points away from the other wire (Newton’s third law pair).

items.stem: Distinguish between the motor effect and electromagnetic induction.
items.answer: In the motor effect a current in a magnetic field produces a force (electrical → mechanical); in induction relative motion or changing flux produces an emf (mechanical → electrical).

items.stem: Design an experiment, using a top-pan balance, to verify that the force on a current-carrying wire is proportional to the current and to determine the flux density between the poles of a magnet. Include the variables, the graph and the main sources of uncertainty.
items.answer: Independent variable: current I (varied with a rheostat, measured with an ammeter); dependent: change in balance reading Δm; control: length of wire in the field, orientation (90°), magnet. Plot Δm g against I: a straight line through the origin confirms F ∝ I; gradient = BL, so B = gradient/L. Uncertainties: length of wire in the field (field not uniform at edges), heating of the wire changes resistance (current drift), balance resolution; reverse the current to cancel systematic offsets.
items.markingKey: Variables identified (A1); method of measuring force (A1); graph and gradient = BL (M1 A1); two valid uncertainty sources with improvements (R1 R1).

items.stem: "Redefining the ampere in terms of the elementary charge (2019) was an improvement over the parallel-wire definition." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: An improvement: tying units to fixed constants makes them universal and stable, although the old definition remains useful for teaching (NOS: measurement standards evolve).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the new definition is based on an invariant constant of nature; it can be realised by single-electron devices and links electrical units to quantum standards. Arguments against: the old definition was conceptually simple and familiar; practical realisation of the new definition is technically demanding. Supported judgement: An improvement: tying units to fixed constants makes them universal and stable, although the old definition remains useful for teaching (NOS: measurement standards evolve). Markbands (15 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "velocity selector".
items.answer: Crossed electric and magnetic fields that allow only particles with speed v = E/B to pass undeflected
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: crossed electric and magnetic fields that allow only particles with speed v = E/B to pass undeflected. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "deflecting plates"?
options: A device that produces a beam of electrons by thermionic emission from a hot cathode and accelerates them through a potential difference
An instrument that separates ions by their mass-to-charge ratio using the radius of their circular paths in a magnetic field
The force F = BIL sin θ on a length L of wire carrying current I at angle θ to a magnetic field B
A pair of parallel plates with a p.d. between them that deflects a beam of charged particles passing between them
items.answer: A pair of parallel plates with a p.d. between them that deflects a beam of charged particles passing between them
items.markingKey: D. "deflecting plates" is a pair of parallel plates with a p.d. between them that deflects a beam of charged particles passing between them.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Fleming's left-hand rule"?
options: A region where a charged particle experiences a constant force qE and so a constant acceleration qE/m
The frequency f = qB/(2πm) at which a charged particle circles in a uniform magnetic field, independent of its speed
The force per unit length F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πr) between two long parallel wires; attractive for currents in the same direction
A rule giving the direction of the force on a current in a magnetic field: First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current, thuMb = Motion (force)
items.answer: A rule giving the direction of the force on a current in a magnetic field: First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current, thuMb = Motion (force)
items.markingKey: D. "Fleming's left-hand rule" is a rule giving the direction of the force on a current in a magnetic field: First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current, thuMb = Motion (force).

items.stem: Distinguish between the force on a charge in a magnetic field and the force on a charge in an electric field.
items.answer: An electric force qE acts on any charge, moving or not, along the field, and can change speed; a magnetic force qvB sin θ acts only on moving charges, perpendicular to v and B, and changes only direction.
items.markingKey: An electric force qE acts on any charge, moving or not, along the field, and can change speed; a magnetic force qvB sin θ acts only on moving charges, perpendicular to v and B, and changes only direction. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Tariq writes: "An electron between deflecting plates follows a circular arc." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A constant force perpendicular to the plates gives a parabolic path; circular paths occur in magnetic fields.
items.markingKey: A constant force perpendicular to the plates gives a parabolic path; circular paths occur in magnetic fields. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the forces between two parallel wires are equal even if the currents are different.
items.answer: The force on wire 2 is B₁I₂L = μ₀I₁I₂L/(2πr) and on wire 1 is B₂I₁L = the same expression; they form a Newton’s third law pair.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The force on wire 2 is B₁I₂L = μ₀I₁I₂L/(2πr) and on wire 1 is B₂I₁L = the same expression; they form a Newton’s third law pair. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The magnetic force on a moving charge is greatest when the velocity is
items.answer: perpendicular to the field
items.markingKey: C. F = qvB sin θ.

items.stem: An electron beam is deflected by a uniform electric field between parallel plates. Predict and explain how the deflection at the exit of the plates changes if the deflecting voltage is doubled.
items.answer: The vertical deflection doubles, because the acceleration eE/m doubles while the time between the plates is unchanged.
items.markingKey: the vertical deflection doubles (A1); the acceleration eE/m doubles while the time between the plates is unchanged (R1).

items.stem: Distinguish between electromagnetic induction and the motor effect.
items.answer: In the motor effect a current in a magnetic field produces a force (electrical → mechanical); in induction relative motion or changing flux produces an emf (mechanical → electrical).
items.markingKey: In the motor effect a current in a magnetic field produces a force (electrical → mechanical); in induction relative motion or changing flux produces an emf (mechanical → electrical). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Crossed fields of E = 5.00 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ and B = 0.05 T form a velocity selector. Which speed passes undeflected?

An electron beam of speed v passes between plates 4.0 cm long and 1.0 cm apart. The vertical deflection y at the exit is measured for different deflecting voltages V. Theory: y = eL²V/(2mₑdv²).

V / V | y / mm
20 | 0.31
40 | 0.62
60 | 0.96
80 | 1.23
100 | 1.56
120 | 1.89

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the speed v of the electrons. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±4 %. State the electron speed with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) y in m (y) against V (x); (b) gradient ≈ 1.57 × 10⁻⁵ m V⁻¹; (c) 2.99 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹; (d) 2.99 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ ± 1 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) y in m (y) against V (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 1.57 × 10⁻⁵ m V⁻¹ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) v = √(eL²/(2mₑd × gradient)) = 2.99 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 4 % of the value = 1 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: A wire 10 cm long carries 2 A at 90° to a 0.5 T field. What is the force on it?
items.markingKey: D. F = BIL sin θ = 0.100 N.

items.stem: In a velocity selector the magnetic flux density is 0.100 T. Calculate the electric field strength needed for deuterons travelling at 1.00 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ to pass undeflected, and explain why the result does not depend on the charge.
items.markingKey: qE = qvB (M1); E = vB = 1.00 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹ (A1); q cancels, so selection depends only on speed (R1).

In an oscilloscope tube, electrons are accelerated through 1500 V, then pass between deflecting plates 3.0 cm long and 1.0 cm apart with 100 V across them. The screen is 15 cm beyond the end of the plates. (a) Calculate the speed of the electrons entering the plates. (b) Calculate the deflection at the exit of the plates. (c) Determine the total deflection on the screen. (d) Explain why doubling the accelerating voltage halves the deflection.
items.markingKey: (a) v = √(2eV/m) = 2.30 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ (A1). (b) a = 1.76 × 10¹⁵ m s⁻², t = 1.31 × 10⁻⁹ s (M1), y = ½at² = 1.50 mm (A1). (c) straight line after plates: extra v_y·D/v (M1); total 16.5 mm (A1). (d) deflection ∝ 1/v² and v² ∝ V_a (R1).

items.stem: Two long parallel wires each carrying 20 A are 10 mm apart; the currents are in the same direction. (a) Calculate the magnetic flux density at one wire due to the other. (b) Determine the force on a 100 cm length of either wire and its direction. (c) A student claims the force would be detectable on a balance reading to 0.01 g. Evaluate this claim. (d) Explain how the forces illustrate Newton’s third law.
items.answer: (a) 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ T; (b) 0.00800 N, attractive; (c) equivalent mass 0.815 g, detectable; (d) equal and opposite forces on the two wires
items.markingKey: (a) B = μ₀I/(2πr) (M1) = 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ T (A1). (b) F = BIL = 0.00800 N (A1), wires attract (A1). (c) F/g = 0.815 g compared with 0.01 g (R1). (d) each wire is in the other’s field; forces equal, opposite, same type (R1).

items.stem: "Mass spectrometry is the most reliable way to identify isotopes." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Very powerful and widely used, but results need careful interpretation; overlaps mean it is best combined with other techniques.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: separates ions by m/q with high precision; needs only tiny samples. Arguments against: ions of the same m/q (e.g. different molecules) can overlap; requires ionisation and vacuum; nuclear methods give different information (e.g. decay). Supported judgement: Very powerful and widely used, but results need careful interpretation; overlaps mean it is best combined with other techniques. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: "Thomson’s cathode-ray experiments discovered the electron." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Thomson is credited because he interpreted measurements as evidence for a universal sub-atomic particle, but discovery built on earlier and later work.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: he measured e/m and showed it was the same for all cathode materials; his interpretation as a universal particle was new. Arguments against: many others (Crookes, Schuster, Kaufmann) worked on cathode rays; the charge was later measured by Millikan; discovery is a process involving a community (NOS). Supported judgement: Thomson is credited because he interpreted measurements as evidence for a universal sub-atomic particle, but discovery built on earlier and later work. Markbands (15 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Define the term "magnetic force on a moving charge".
items.answer: The force F = qvB sin θ on a charge q moving with velocity v at angle θ to a magnetic field B, perpendicular to both v and B

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "force on a current-carrying conductor"?
options: The force F = BIL sin θ on a length L of wire carrying current I at angle θ to a magnetic field B
The force F = qvB sin θ on a charge q moving with velocity v at angle θ to a magnetic field B, perpendicular to both v and B
Crossed electric and magnetic fields that allow only particles with speed v = E/B to pass undeflected
A rule giving the direction of the force on a current in a magnetic field: First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current, thuMb = Motion (force)
items.answer: The force F = BIL sin θ on a length L of wire carrying current I at angle θ to a magnetic field B

items.stem: Hana and a classmate in Oslo disagree about force on a moving charge and the circular motion of charges in magnetic fields. Which statement is correct?
options: Doubling the speed of a proton in a magnetic field doubles its period.
The magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity and does no work, so it cannot change the speed; an electric field is needed.
A stationary electron in a magnetic field experiences a force along the field lines.
A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field is pushed along the field lines.
items.answer: The magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity and does no work, so it cannot change the speed; an electric field is needed.
items.markingKey: B. The other options are common misconceptions. The magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity and does no work, so it cannot change the speed; an electric field is needed.

items.stem: The deflection of an electron beam between deflecting plates is doubled by
items.answer: doubling the deflecting p.d.
items.markingKey: C. y = eVL²/(2mdv²) ∝ V.

items.stem: In an investigation the relationship F = BIL for a wire in the field of a magnet on a top-pan balance as the current I is varied is expected. Explain how a linear graph can be used to verify this relationship and to determine a value from the gradient.
items.answer: Plot F (= Δm g) (y-axis) against I (x-axis); gradient = BL, so B = gradient/L. A line through the origin confirms F ∝ I.
items.markingKey: Correct choice of axes: F (= Δm g) against I (M1); straight line expected (R1); gradient = BL, so B = gradient/L (A1). A line through the origin confirms F ∝ I.

items.stem: An electron and a proton enter the same magnetic field perpendicularly with the same speed. Which is correct?
options: they curve in opposite directions and the electron’s radius is much smaller
they curve the same way with equal radii
items.answer: they curve in opposite directions and the electron’s radius is much smaller
items.markingKey: A. Opposite charges; r ∝ m.

items.stem: Explain why gravitational effects can be neglected for electrons in a cathode-ray tube.
items.answer: The electric force eE (~10⁻¹⁵ N for E ~10⁴ V m⁻¹) is about 10¹⁴ times larger than the weight mₑg (~9 × 10⁻³⁰ N).

items.stem: Isabel is revising force on a current-carrying conductor and between parallel wires. Which of the following statements is correct?

A magnetic field can be used to speed up an electron beam.
An electron moves in the direction of the electric field lines.

items.markingKey: B. The other options are common misconceptions. Both wires feel the same force μ₀I₁I₂L/(2πr), by Newton’s third law.

items.stem: An electron is projected at 4.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ along the direction of a uniform electric field of 500 V m⁻¹. (a) Determine how far it travels before coming momentarily to rest. (b) Determine the time taken. (c) Explain what happens next and how the answers change for a proton with the same initial speed.
